subject: english
chapter_title: The World is too Much With Us

concepts.title: Getting and Spending: Humanity Out of Tune with Nature
concepts.definition: Wordsworth's sonnet indicts his age: the world is too much with us -- late and soon, getting and spending, we lay waste our powers. Humanity has given its heart away in exchange, and no longer sees the sea that bares its bosom to the moon or the winds that howl at all hours.
concepts.key_idea: Material appetite deafens -- humanity trades its heart for commerce and goes out of tune with sea and wind.
concepts.textbook_ref: keww115.txt octave (world too much with us, getting and spending, laying waste our powers, sea that bares her bosom, winds howling, out of tune)
question_patterns: what does wordsworth mean by the world is too much with us
in class 11 the world is too much with us: explain getting and spending we lay waste our powers

solution_steps.explain: The material world -- getting and spending -- consumes human powers that should belong to nature and spirit.
The roaring sea and howling winds, nature's drama, no longer move people who are out of tune with them.
The heart has been sold for commerce -- a bargain the sonnet calls ruinous.

concepts.title: Proteus and Triton: The Pagan Remedy
concepts.definition: The sestet turns to mythology: the pagan Greeks, suckled in a creed outworn, glimpsed gods in nature -- Proteus rising from the sea, Triton blowing his wreathed horn. The poet would rather be a pagan so attired than stand now, out of tune, beholding a nature stripped of divinity and so sordidly forsworn.
concepts.key_idea: Better an old creed that sees gods in waves than a new one that sees only goods -- myth as the lost vision of nature.
concepts.textbook_ref: keww115.txt sestet (pagan suckled in a creed outworn, proteus rising from the sea, triton's wreathed horn, glimpses that would cheer)
question_patterns: why does the poet wish to be a pagan
in class 11 the world is too much with us: who are proteus and triton
what does the poet mean by a creed outworn
how would glimpses of proteus and triton cheer the poet

what is the significance of the mythological allusions

solution_steps.explain: The old religion imagined divinity inside nature -- seas and winds alive with gods.
Proteus rising from the sea and Triton sounding his wreathed horn would be 'glimpses' to cheer a forlorn soul.
The poet prefers even an outworn creed that animates nature to a modern sightlessness that forswears all wonder.

concepts.title: Sonnet Form as Argument: Octave Accusation, Sestet Longing
concepts.definition: The poem's Petrarchan shape carries its logic: the octave states the accusation -- a humanity wasting its powers in commerce, deaf to nature -- while the sestet answers with longing, the pagan wish and the mythological vision. The turn (volta) between them is the poem's hinge.
concepts.key_idea: Form as argument -- accusation in the octave, yearning in the sestet, and a volta between them.

solution_steps.explain: Eight lines lay out the charge: materialism has deadened humanity to nature's life.
Six lines answer with the pagan remedy -- Proteus, Triton and the wish to feel again.
The volta turns accusation into longing, making the form itself the poem's argument.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Explain 'getting and spending, we lay waste our powers' as the key accusation of the poem.

solution_template.explain: Getting and spending names an economy of endless acquisition and consumption.
Human powers -- feeling, imagination, sympathy -- are squandered in that cycle.
Deafened by commerce, humanity no longer hears the sea and winds that still sing -- the heart gone for exchange.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Why does the poet call the pagan creed 'outworn' yet prefer it to his own age?

solution_template.explain: Scientifically the creed is outdated -- no one now believes Proteus rises from the sea.
Yet it saw nature as alive and divine, where the modern age sees only resource and commodity.
Wordsworth's paradox: a false belief that keeps wonder alive is better than a true sightlessness.
